recent_posts.title: Using AI to automate small repetitive tasks
recent_posts.summary: A short personal account of using Claude Code to automate a tedious file-renaming task: reading text from flash cards in video frames, looking up codes in a Google Sheet, and renaming hundreds of video files automatically. The author highlights that AI is useful not just for building full products but for handling small, repetitive, boring tasks quickly and reliably.

recent_posts.title: How one developer uses AI coding tools without eroding their skills
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares their personal workflow for using AI coding tools without losing core programming skills. The approach distinguishes between vibe coding personal tools and prototypes (no code review needed) versus production code (100% review, ~50% written manually). Claude Code is used for well-isolated 'omega mess' components that can be thoroughly tested. The post includes a concrete case study of adding a pro voice feature to a boxing app, showing how planning, legacy code handling, AI-assisted generation, and manual UI coding were combined. The author argues that the time saved by AI should be redirected toward deeper thinking rather than shipping more features.

recent_posts.title: Hiring Tech Leaders: Think in Spectrums, Not Checkboxes
recent_posts.summary: Hiring senior tech leaders like CTOs and VPs of Engineering is difficult because experienced candidates know all the textbook answers. Instead of evaluating right vs. wrong responses, the key is mapping candidates on behavioral spectrums — such as consensus-driven vs. decisive, hands-on vs. strategic, or risk-averse vs. risk-tolerant. By defining acceptable ranges on these sliders before interviewing, hiring managers can assess whether a candidate's natural leadership style fits the company's current stage and needs. The best candidates have a default style but can adapt within limits; pushing too far from their comfort zone leads to burnout or regression. The framework also helps when choosing between imperfect candidates by understanding the tradeoffs and compensating with complementary hires or coaching.

recent_posts.title: Minimum Viable Post Mortem Process
recent_posts.summary: A lightweight post-mortem process designed for small engineering teams (under 20 engineers) who have no existing incident review workflow. The approach covers: creating a dedicated incident chat channel, writing a short document capturing cause, impact, and resolution, identifying preventive actions split into immediate vs. deferred tasks, scheduling follow-up reviews at 1 week and 1 month, and sharing findings with the team. The guide explicitly lists the shortcuts taken (no metrics, no timeline, no incident prioritization, no formal incident leader) and explains why a simple imperfect process beats having nothing. Blameless culture is emphasized throughout.

recent_posts.title: Why technical brilliance without collaboration skills is a net negative
recent_posts.summary: Explores the common pattern of 'brilliant jerk' engineers who are technically skilled but bring negative value to teams through poor collaboration, abrasive behavior, and refusal to follow team norms. Argues that raw intelligence is overrated compared to the ability to work well with others, and that managers must both acknowledge valid criticism from such individuals while helping them adjust their approach to become genuine force multipliers.

recent_posts.title: My Experience with Liquid Glass so Far
recent_posts.summary: An iOS developer shares first-hand experience migrating three apps to iOS 26 and its new Liquid Glass design system. The author generally likes the new aesthetic, noting it gives native apps a more distinct look compared to web apps, and finds the migration easier for newer, simpler apps. Key challenges include significant performance regressions in beta2 (apps taking up to a minute to boot), battery drain issues, UI blinking caused by mixed light/dark photo content conflicting with the adaptive glass elements, and the need to refactor custom SwiftUI components that block adoption of new glass button styles. Practical migration advice is offered: start testing on a secondary device now, remove overly custom components, and don't rush full Liquid Glass adoption before September but plan for it inevitably.

recent_posts.title: Building an App to Find Highway Stops
recent_posts.summary: A solo developer shares the process of building and shipping a niche iOS app for finding French highway rest stops in under two weeks. The post covers the use case motivation, MVP scoping decisions, UI choices using native SwiftUI and MapKit, an offline-first data strategy using community-sourced open data, AdMob monetization experiments, and post-launch results (~1000 downloads, €0.20–0.70/day in ad revenue). Key learnings include MapKit being more capable than expected, AdMob being unpleasant to integrate, and the offline data approach proving viable given how rarely highway data changes.

recent_posts.title: How one overlooked UX detail affected 70% of fitness app users
recent_posts.summary: A solo developer shares a UX lesson learned while redesigning a boxing fitness app. After improving the pause button placement, analytics revealed that over 70% of new users still tapped random screen areas first — a behavior common in video apps. The developer initially dismissed tap-to-pause as a minor detail not worth implementing, but data proved it was a major user expectation. The takeaway: small UX details can be critical, especially in physical contexts like workouts, and user observation plus data tracking are essential for catching overlooked assumptions.

recent_posts.title: Three types of power for tech leads and managers
recent_posts.summary: A concise framework for understanding the three types of power in tech organizations: expertise power (knowledge-based influence), relational power (relationship-based influence), and role power (authority-based influence). New technical leads often struggle because they lack role power, while new managers may over-rely on it. The post argues that frequently using role power in tech companies is a sign of failure — good managers should primarily leverage expertise and relational power to get things done.

recent_posts.title: Controlling the Blast Radius
recent_posts.summary: Engineering managers shouldn't aim to prevent all mistakes — instead, they should create safe conditions for failure by 'controlling the blast radius.' Borrowing from cybersecurity, this means finding a middle ground between hands-off and hands-on management: granting team members autonomy while putting guardrails in place so that failures remain recoverable. Practical examples cover scenarios like meeting deadlines, risky releases, vendor selection, and onboarding new hires, showing how the right level of involvement varies by context, seniority, and stakes.
